difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain (new compound → enzyme suppression → reduced inflammation). The weakener attacks the move from lab results to clinical conclusion. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope comparison to another drug.
stimulus: A pharmaceutical researcher found that a newly synthesized compound suppresses the production of an enzyme linked to chronic joint inflammation. In trials on laboratory mice, mice administered the compound showed significantly lower levels of joint inflammation than untreated mice. The researcher concluded that the compound will effectively reduce chronic joint inflammation in human patients.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enzyme suppressed by the compound plays a substantially different role in human joint tissue than it does in mouse joint tissue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several existing anti-inflammatory drugs also work by suppressing enzyme production.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The laboratory mice used in the trials were specially bred to develop joint inflammation rapidly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The compound suppressed enzyme production in all treated mice, not just those with chronic inflammation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human patients with chronic joint inflammation typically have higher baseline enzyme levels than healthy individuals.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes that because the compound works on mice, it will work on humans — a direct analogical leap. If the enzyme plays a different role in human tissue, the mechanism that reduced inflammation in mice may not translate, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the analogy from mouse to human by exposing a disanalogy in the underlying mechanism.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The fact that other drugs work similarly neither strengthens nor weakens this compound's human efficacy.
explanations.C: This could, if anything, raise concerns about the trial's representativeness, but it doesn't directly attack the conclusion about human patients — it's too narrow a methodological quibble to undermine the conclusion.
explanations.D: Irrelevant to the human-efficacy conclusion. Universal suppression in mice doesn't bear on whether the compound will work in humans.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Higher baseline enzyme levels in affected humans might actually support the idea that suppressing the enzyme would benefit human patients.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument resting on a two-step chain: carbon tax → higher energy costs → reduced consumption. Weakener attacks the second step. One distractor strengthens; one attacks a peripheral claim.
stimulus: An economist argued that the federal government's newly enacted carbon tax will significantly reduce the nation's overall energy consumption. The tax raises the price of fossil-fuel-derived energy, and consumers and businesses consistently reduce their consumption of goods and services when prices rise. Therefore, the carbon tax will achieve its goal of meaningfully lowering total energy use nationwide.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the argument's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most economists agree that carbon taxes are among the most efficient tools for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For the majority of consumers and businesses, fossil-fuel-derived energy has no readily available substitute, making demand for it highly inelastic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The carbon tax is projected to generate billions of dollars in annual government revenue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several other nations have enacted carbon taxes at higher rates than the one now in effect in this country.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Businesses that produce renewable energy are expected to benefit financially from the carbon tax.

explanations.correct: The argument assumes the standard economic principle that price increases reduce consumption. If demand for fossil-fuel energy is highly inelastic — meaning consumers and businesses cannot easily cut back or switch — then higher prices will not produce meaningful reductions in consumption, directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Strengthener trap. Expert agreement on carbon taxes' efficiency supports, rather than weakens, the economist's claim.
explanations.B: Correct. Inelastic demand breaks the link between higher prices and reduced consumption — the key inferential step.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Revenue generation is a separate outcome; it doesn't speak to whether energy consumption will fall.
explanations.D: Unwarranted comparison trap. What other nations do at different rates doesn't bear on whether this tax will reduce domestic consumption.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Renewable energy producers' financial gains are a side effect; they don't address whether total energy consumption declines.

difficultyReason: Causal argument with an alternative-explanation weakener. The stimulus infers cause from correlation. One distractor attacks a peripheral premise; one is an irrelevant historical fact.
stimulus: A city's transportation authority reported that after a new light-rail line opened, traffic congestion on the two parallel highway corridors decreased by 22 percent over the following year. The authority concluded that the light-rail line was responsible for the reduction in highway congestion.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The light-rail line's opening was accompanied by a major increase in gasoline prices that prompted many commuters to abandon their cars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ridership on the new light-rail line exceeded the authority's projections by 30 percent in its first year of operation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several businesses along the two highway corridors closed during the year following the light-rail line's opening.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The light-rail line cost significantly more to construct than the authority had initially budgeted.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Other cities that have opened light-rail lines have reported similar reductions in highway congestion.

explanations.correct: The authority infers that the light-rail line caused the congestion decrease because the two events coincided. Introducing a simultaneous gasoline price spike — an independent factor that would also reduce highway traffic — provides an alternative explanation for the observed decrease, weakening the causal conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Alternative explanation that accounts for the congestion drop without crediting the light-rail line.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. High ridership is consistent with the light-rail line drawing cars off the road, supporting the authority's conclusion.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Business closures could reduce traffic, but this is a weaker and less direct alternative explanation than A; moreover, it doesn't clearly undermine the rail line as the primary cause without further inference.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Construction cost overruns have no bearing on whether the rail line caused the congestion reduction.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Analogous outcomes in other cities support, rather than weaken, the authority's causal claim.

difficultyReason: Analogical/predictive argument in law. The weakener identifies a disanalogy between the two legal contexts compared. Distractors include a strengthener and an out-of-scope procedural fact.
stimulus: A legal scholar argued that the nation's courts should recognize a constitutional right to digital privacy in personal communications, citing the precedent established in Katz v. United States, in which the Supreme Court held that individuals have a reasonable expectation of privacy in telephone conversations. Because digital communications are functionally equivalent to telephone conversations as a means of private personal exchange, the scholar concluded that courts should extend the same constitutional protection to digital communications.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most calls into question the scholar's reasoning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike the contents of a telephone call, digital communications are routinely stored on third-party servers and disclosed to those servers' operators under standard user agreements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Supreme Court in Katz v. United States unanimously agreed that some form of privacy protection was warranted for telephone calls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Several foreign legal systems already extend explicit privacy protections to digital communications.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Digital communications can travel across international borders, complicating jurisdictional questions.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have become increasingly comfortable applying precedents established before the digital era to contemporary technological contexts.

explanations.correct: The scholar's argument rests on the analogy that digital communications are functionally equivalent to telephone calls for constitutional purposes. If digital communications are routinely stored on and disclosed to third-party servers — a key disanalogy — users may lack a 'reasonable expectation of privacy,' which is the very standard Katz established. This disanalogy undercuts the analogical extension.
explanations.A: Correct. Exposes a legally significant disanalogy: the third-party disclosure doctrine (established in Smith v. Maryland) applies to digital communications in a way it did not apply to Katz's phone call, undermining the functional equivalence claim.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Unanimous agreement in Katz reinforces the precedent the scholar is relying on.
explanations.C: Out of scope. Foreign legal systems' practices don't bear on what domestic courts should do under the U.S. Constitution.
explanations.D: Shift in subject. Jurisdictional complexity is a separate problem, not one that undermines the analogical argument about whether privacy rights should exist.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Courts' comfort with applying older precedents to new technology supports the scholar's approach.

difficultyReason: Two-step causal chain in environmental science: deforestation → soil erosion → river sedimentation. Weakener attacks the second causal link. One distractor attacks the first link only; one is a strengthener.
stimulus: Environmental officials in the Maren River watershed documented a 40 percent increase in riverside deforestation over the past decade. They concluded that this deforestation is responsible for the severe sedimentation recently observed in the Maren River, reasoning that deforestation leads to soil erosion, and soil erosion delivers excess sediment into adjacent waterways.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The deforested areas in the Maren River watershed are separated from the river by wide bands of intact wetland vegetation that trap eroded soil before it reaches the river.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Soil erosion rates in the Maren River watershed have increased sharply over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Deforestation in neighboring watersheds has not led to measurable increases in river sedimentation in those areas.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Maren River has experienced periodic sedimentation events caused by upstream flooding throughout its recorded history.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Government agencies have logged the deforested areas under permits that require replanting within five years.

explanations.correct: Even if deforestation causes soil erosion (first link), the conclusion that this erosion reaches and sediments the river depends on a second link: eroded soil actually enters the river. If intact wetland buffers trap the eroded soil before it reaches the river, the second causal step fails, and the sedimentation must have another cause.
explanations.A: Correct. Severs the second causal link — from soil erosion to river sedimentation — by introducing a physical barrier that prevents eroded soil from reaching the river.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Confirming increased erosion supports the causal chain rather than weakening it.
explanations.C: Too narrow / shifts subject. Evidence from neighboring watersheds introduces an alternative comparison but does not directly explain why the erosion-to-sedimentation link fails in the Maren watershed.
explanations.D: Out of scope. Historical periodic sedimentation from flooding is a different phenomenon and doesn't undermine the officials' specific causal claim about recent deforestation.
explanations.E: Irrelevant. Future replanting commitments don't bear on whether past or current deforestation caused the observed sedimentation.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument in technology policy. The weakener shows the predicted mechanism will not operate as assumed. Distractors include an out-of-scope historical analogy and a strengthener.
stimulus: A technology policy analyst predicted that mandating open-source software in all government agencies will substantially lower the agencies' long-term software costs. The analyst reasoned that open-source software eliminates licensing fees, which currently constitute the largest share of government software expenditure, and that the money saved on fees can be redirected to other priorities.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the analyst's prediction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Open-source software typically requires significantly more specialized technical staff to maintain and customize than commercial licensed software, and qualified personnel are costly to hire and retain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Several private corporations have successfully reduced their software costs by transitioning to open-source solutions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Government agencies are subject to procurement regulations that may delay the adoption of new software platforms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Open-source software communities regularly release security updates, reducing the risk of cyberattacks on government systems.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Licensing fees for commercial software have increased at an average annual rate of 8 percent over the past decade.

explanations.correct: The analyst assumes that eliminating licensing fees translates directly into lower overall costs. If open-source software requires expensive specialized personnel whose costs offset or exceed the savings on licensing fees, the predicted net cost reduction fails — directly undermining the conclusion.
explanations.A: Correct. Introduces offsetting costs (personnel) that the analyst's reasoning ignores, attacking the move from 'no licensing fees' to 'lower long-term costs.'
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Corporate success with open-source solutions supports the analyst's prediction by analogy.
explanations.C: Too narrow. Procurement delays affect the timing of adoption, not whether long-term costs will ultimately be lower — so it doesn't squarely undermine the cost-savings conclusion.
explanations.D: Strengthener trap. Security benefits are an additional advantage of open-source, reinforcing the case for the mandate.
explanations.E: Strengthener trap. Rising licensing fees make the savings from eliminating them even more significant, supporting the analyst's prediction.

difficultyReason: Causal argument in history/policy based on a correlation. The weakener provides an alternative historical explanation. One distractor is an accurate but irrelevant detail; one strengthens.
stimulus: Historians studying the decline of the Roman Empire have noted that a series of severe grain shortages struck the empire's western provinces in the decades immediately preceding the final collapse of Roman authority in 476 CE. One prominent historian concluded that these grain shortages were the primary cause of the empire's fall, since a starving population cannot sustain the military and administrative apparatus necessary to maintain state authority.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grain shortages affected the eastern provinces of the Roman Empire less severely than the western provinces.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The final collapse of Roman authority in the western provinces coincided with a massive influx of Gothic and Hunnic military forces that overwhelmed the Roman legions independently of any economic crisis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ancient grain storage facilities in the western provinces had deteriorated significantly by the fourth century CE.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Historians disagree about the precise date on which Roman authority in the west should be considered to have ended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Grain shortages of comparable severity had occurred in earlier centuries without preventing Roman military campaigns.

explanations.correct: The historian concludes the grain shortages were the primary cause of the collapse. If a massive independent military invasion — unrelated to the economic crisis — overwhelmed the legions, then military defeat, not starvation, could be the primary cause, providing a powerful alternative explanation that undermines the historian's causal claim.
explanations.A: Out of scope. The differential impact on eastern vs. western provinces is consistent with the historian's argument; it doesn't provide an alternative cause.
explanations.B: Correct. A simultaneous, independent military catastrophe constitutes an alternative explanation for the collapse that competes with the grain shortage hypothesis.
explanations.C: Accurate but irrelevant trap. Deteriorated storage might have worsened shortages, but it doesn't undermine the conclusion — it actually supports the causal chain.
explanations.D: Irrelevant. Disagreement about the collapse's precise date doesn't address the causal claim about grain shortages.
explanations.E: This is a genuine weakener but a weaker one than B: if shortages didn't cause collapse before, it suggests shortages alone aren't sufficient — but it doesn't provide a positive alternative explanation for the fifth-century collapse. B more directly undermines the 'primary cause' claim.

difficultyReason: Generalization from a sample in linguistics research. The weakener attacks the representativeness of the sample. Distractors include a strengthener and a shift-in-subject trap.
stimulus: A linguist studied a group of 200 bilingual children raised in households where both English and Spanish were spoken and found that these children reached all standard language-acquisition milestones at the same ages as monolingual English-speaking children. The linguist concluded that bilingual upbringing does not delay language development in children generally.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The 200 children studied came exclusively from households with highly educated parents who engaged in frequent, structured language activities with their children — conditions rarely found in the broader population of bilingual households.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Monolingual children in the study's comparison group were drawn from the same geographic region as the bilingual children.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bilingual children in the study scored higher than monolingual children on tests measuring vocabulary breadth in their dominant language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Some researchers have argued that early bilingual exposure enhances cognitive flexibility in children.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Language-acquisition milestones are defined differently by different professional organizations, making cross-study comparisons difficult.

explanations.correct: The linguist generalizes from a sample to 'children generally.' If the sample was drawn exclusively from unusually favorable conditions — highly educated, engaged parents — it is not representative of the broader bilingual population, where developmental delays might still occur. This attacks the generalization's validity.
explanations.A: Correct. Reveals a sampling bias that makes the general conclusion unreliable.
explanations.B: Strengthener trap. Matching the comparison group geographically reduces a confound and supports the study's validity.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Superior vocabulary scores in bilingual children further support the argument that bilingual upbringing poses no developmental disadvantage.
explanations.D: Shift in subject trap. Claims about cognitive flexibility are a different outcome than language-acquisition milestones; this doesn't weaken the conclusion about milestone timing.
explanations.E: Too narrow. Definitional disagreements complicate comparisons but don't directly undermine the study's internal finding or the generalization drawn from it.

difficultyReason: Predictive argument in arts/policy. The weakener attacks the assumption that the proposed mechanism will produce the predicted effect. One distractor is an irrelevant economic fact; one is a strengthener.
stimulus: The director of a regional arts council argued that offering substantial cash grants to independent theaters will increase attendance at live theatrical performances across the region. The director reasoned that the grants will allow theaters to reduce ticket prices, and lower ticket prices will attract larger audiences who were previously deterred by cost.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the director's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Surveys of residents who do not attend live theater indicate that the primary barrier to attendance is unfamiliarity with theatrical programming, not ticket prices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Independent theaters in the region have struggled financially for the past several years due to rising operating costs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cash grants of the size proposed have successfully revitalized performing arts sectors in two comparable regions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Regional arts councils in other areas have funded grant programs for museums and symphony orchestras with positive results.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some independent theaters plan to use grant funds primarily to upgrade their facilities rather than to reduce ticket prices.

explanations.correct: The director's argument depends on a two-step mechanism: grants → lower prices → higher attendance. If non-attendees stay away because of unfamiliarity, not cost, then lowering prices will not attract them, breaking the second causal link and directly undermining the predicted attendance increase.
explanations.A: Correct. Attacks the assumption that price is the key barrier to attendance, severing the link between lower prices and higher audiences.
explanations.B: Out of scope. The theaters' prior financial struggles explain why grants are needed but don't undermine whether grants will produce the predicted attendance increase.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Comparable success elsewhere supports the director's prediction.
explanations.D: Shift in subject trap. Grants to museums and orchestras are a different context; the results don't speak to independent theater attendance.
explanations.E: This weakens the first step (grants → lower prices) in part, but it says 'some' theaters — leaving open that others will reduce prices. It is a weaker attack than A, which undermines the mechanism even if prices do drop.

difficultyReason: Ethical/policy argument based on an analogy between two regulatory contexts. Weakener identifies a relevant disanalogy. One distractor strengthens; one is an accurate but irrelevant fact about one side of the analogy.
stimulus: A consumer-advocacy group argued that ride-sharing drivers should be classified as employees rather than independent contractors, citing the precedent set when delivery couriers at a major logistics company were reclassified as employees after regulators determined that the company exercised sufficient control over their working conditions. Because ride-sharing platforms similarly dictate drivers' pricing, routes, and performance standards, the advocacy group concluded that ride-sharing drivers meet the same legal standard for employee classification.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Unlike delivery couriers, who were required to work designated shifts set by the logistics company, ride-sharing drivers can log on and off the platform at any time of their choosing and are subject to no minimum hour requirements.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The logistics company's delivery couriers were found to receive compensation below the legal minimum wage before their reclassification.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ride-sharing platforms collect data on driver behavior, including speed and route adherence, to enforce their performance standards.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Employee classification would entitle ride-sharing drivers to benefits such as health insurance and unemployment compensation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several jurisdictions have already enacted legislation specifically addressing the employment status of gig-economy workers.

explanations.correct: The advocacy group's argument rests on an analogy between delivery couriers and ride-sharing drivers. The legal standard for employee classification typically includes control over scheduling and hours as a central factor. If ride-sharing drivers have complete freedom over when they work — unlike the couriers who had mandatory shifts — this is a legally significant disanalogy that undermines the conclusion that they meet the same classification standard.
explanations.A: Correct. Identifies a key disanalogy in the degree of control exercised, specifically regarding scheduling autonomy, which is central to the legal test being applied.
explanations.B: Irrelevant. The couriers' wage violation was a separate basis for their reclassification that doesn't apply to the ride-sharing context being argued about.
explanations.C: Strengthener trap. Evidence that platforms monitor and enforce performance standards supports the advocacy group's claim that control is exercised over drivers.
explanations.D: Out of scope. The entitlements that would flow from reclassification are a consequence, not a reason bearing on whether the legal standard is met.
explanations.E: Out of scope. Legislation in other jurisdictions is a separate legal development; it doesn't speak to whether ride-sharing drivers meet the specific standard used in the courier precedent.
